2027 BMW i3 50 xDrive Spends Fewer Than 3 Hours Charging on Its Way From Norway to Spain
8 photos
Photo: BMW
Driving a zero-emission car from the top of Norway to southern Spain involves more than sufficient battery capacity to cover the distance. From the route between charging stations to traffic and weather conditions, a lot of things can make a substantial difference between the time spent driving and charging.
BMW wanted to demonstrate how its latest electric vehicle technologies can handle those variables by sending a production-spec i3 50 xDrive on the Paneuropeana route, which involves covering 5,886.7 kilometers (3,658 miles) across eight countries. On its route, the i3 50 xDrive in question required merely 2 hours, 45 minutes, and 54 seconds of DC fast charging.
The journey started at North Cape on the Norwegian island of Mageroya, where a headland extends into the Arctic Ocean. At the other end of the route, the full-electric Bimmer reached Tarifa in Spain's Andalusian province of Cadiz. In other words, the southernmost point of mainland Europe. A considerable geographical spread, for sure, with said route connecting two very different places.
North Cape and Tarifa couldn't be much farther apart within continental Europe, and this journey is all the more relevant because it subjected the i3 50 xDrive to a variety of road and weather conditions along the way. BMW claims the subject vehicle covered ordinary country roads, motorways, and urban stretches, with the organizers choosing checkpoints that prioritize normal road use instead of speed.
All in all, the team had to balance three distinct variables: driving distance, energy consumption, and charging performance. The objective here wasn't to achieve the shortest possible journey time at any cost, but to minimize the accumulated time connected to chargers.
Photo: BMW The i3 in question spent a whopping 3 days, 2 hours, and 41 minutes actually driving, whereas the chargers used along the way filled up the high-voltage battery of the 50 xDrive at an average of 275 kilowatts. Better still, the Bavarian automaker quotes 12.5 kilowatt-hours for every 100 kilometers (62 miles) as the average energy consumption on this route, which is below the WLTP-rated consumption range of 13.4 to 18.0 kWh/100 km.
Average speed? Make that 79.7 kilometers per hour, which is 49.5 miles per hour in the United Kingdom and the United States of America. The Munich-based manufacturer also claims this result beats the Paneuropeana charging time record from 2017 by more than seven hours, with the previous record holder being a Tesla Model S 100D that clocked 9 hours and 51 minutes.
Under the skin, the i3 50 xDrive packs two electric drive units with combined maximum output ratings of 463 horsepower and 476 pound-feet (645 Newton-meters) of twist, enabling the compact luxury sedan to hit 100 kilometers per hour (62 miles per hour) in 4.7 seconds. Capable of hitting 200 kph (124 mph), the i3 50 xDrive is rocking 108.7 kilowatt-hours of usable capacity.
Benefiting from a cell-to-pack architecture, said high-voltage battery uses cylindrical cells instead of the previous-gen prismatic design. The 800-volt electrical system and this gen-six battery enable a maximum DC charging power of 400 kilowatts, with BMW claiming that 10 minutes of charging on direct current will get you 423 kilometers (263 miles) of WLTP range.
